evals.prompt: Running DriftCon Build Weekend in three weeks. We expect 48 teams to submit. Demo structure is already locked: expo tables, and our ops lead budgeted 5 minutes of judge time per team. Submission closes at 15:30 and the ceremony starts at 17:00. I have 9 judges confirmed. Northwind, our platform sponsor, offered to send 6 more people, so with 15 judges every judge can walk all 48 tables and we get a properly comparable field. Can you lay out how we run the judging round?
evals.expected_output: A judging plan that computes the full-coverage ceiling first, shows the 48-team field is already past it, refuses the premise that extra judges restore full coverage, computes judges-per-team for both judge counts, and lands on a sampled panel with per-judge normalization plus a named allocation map.
expectations: States the full-coverage ceiling as N <= W / t and computes 90 / 5 = 18 teams
States that 48 teams exceeds that 18-team ceiling, so full coverage is impossible
States explicitly that the full-coverage ceiling contains no judge-count term, so adding judges cannot extend it
Refuses the user's premise that recruiting 6 more judges lets every judge see every team
Computes judges per team as k = floor((9 x 90) / (48 x 5)) = 3
Identifies the allocation band as a sampled panel band (Band 2), not full coverage and not triage
Recomputes k for 15 judges as 5 and states full coverage is still impossible at that judge count
Prescribes per-judge normalization rather than a raw average, because judges score a proper subset of the field
Delivers the allocation map as a named list giving judge, teams, visiting order and start time
Notes the 5-minute expo figure allows nothing for setup or swap, so the ceiling is an optimistic upper bound rather than a capacity promise
Reserves buffer time rather than allocating 100% of the 90-minute window
Does not propose any prize amount or prize split

evals.prompt: We badly misjudged demand at Kestrel Hack. 210 teams submitted. Expo judging, 4 minutes of judge time per team, and we have exactly 100 minutes between submission close and the ceremony, which is contractually fixed because the venue hands the hall back at 18:00. Seven judges showed up out of the eleven who said yes. My plan is to cut each visit down to 90 seconds and push the judges to move fast. Tell me how to make that work.
evals.expected_output: A plan that computes the triage threshold, shows even one judge per team does not fit, refuses the on-the-day shortening of the per-team slot, and designs a published pass/fail pre-screen followed by a finals round re-checked against the remaining window.
expectations: Computes the triage threshold as (J x W) / t = (7 x 100) / 4 = 175 teams
States 210 exceeds 175, so not even one judge per team fits the window
Names this as the triage band (Band 3), not merely an expensive plan
Refuses to shorten the per-team judging time on the day
Gives the reason that shortening t mid-round re-scores whichever teams were seen first
Prescribes triage-then-finals as the only live-window allocation available in this band
Specifies the first round as a pass/fail gate, never a score
Bases the gate on published submission requirements such as whether it runs, whether it meets the brief's deliverable format, and whether it is eligible
States the pre-screen and its criteria must be published in the brief before submissions close
Sizes the finalist slate from the remaining window W2 after the pre-screen consumes part of W, not from the original 100 minutes
Re-runs the k >= 1 feasibility check on the surviving finalist count and the remaining window
Names a longer window or a format change, decided before the event, as the only legitimate responses if the finals round also fails the gate

evals.prompt: Small one this year: Larkfield Hack has 14 teams submitting. Judging is a 120-minute block, 8 minutes of judge time per team, 5 judges. Two things. First, one of our judges is famously severe - last year he gave almost everything about two points below where the others landed on our 1-5 sheets. Our data person wants to z-score every judge's sheet before combining so that gets washed out. Second, four of the five judges are catching trains straight after their last table, so whatever we do has to not need them in a room together. What's the setup?
evals.expected_output: A plan that confirms full coverage fits, explains why normalization is pure overhead in that case, recommends a raw average, deletes synchronous consensus given the departing judges, and refuses re-scoring and organizer override.
expectations: Computes 120 / 8 = 15 and confirms 14 teams fits under full coverage
States normalization buys nothing and is pure overhead under full coverage
Explains that a uniformly harsh judge adds the same constant to every team they score, so under full coverage the ordering is untouched
Recommends a raw average as the combination rule for this band
States the general rule that normalization applies when a judge scored a proper subset of the field
Fixes and writes down the combination rule before scoring opens rather than after seeing results
Notes normalization corrects a uniformly harsh judge but cannot correct a judge harsh on one kind of project and generous on another
Deletes synchronous consensus as an option because judges leave straight after their slot
States full coverage needs no allocation map beyond a start order
States the efficiency ordering in this band puts raw average ahead of per-judge normalization and synchronous consensus
Does not offer an organizer override of the judges' combined result as an option
Does not propose re-scoring or a second judging pass

evals.prompt: Problem. Northwind Cloud is funding our AI track at Hollowbrook Hack and clause 7 of the signed agreement says their VP of Developer Products sits on the jury for that track. My co-organizer's fix is that she sits there, we let her fill in a sheet, and then we quietly drop her column before we compute the winner so it's clean. Nobody outside the three of us would know. The rules page is still open for edits until submissions close next Friday. What should we actually do?
evals.expected_output: A plan that accepts the contractual conflict rather than recusing it away, confines the sponsor judge to her own track, pairs her with a neutral, runs a drop-test openly, and discloses the composition in the published rules before submissions close.
expectations: States the conflict was accepted at contract time and overrides the conflict-of-interest ladder rather than being recusable
Refuses the proposal to quietly discard the sponsor judge's scores
Confines the sponsor judge to the track her company funds
Keeps the sponsor judge off the overall or grand-prize decision
Pairs the sponsor judge with at least one neutral judge on that track
Runs a drop-test computing the track rank both with and without her scores
States that if the winner is unchanged, that is recorded in the announcement notes
States that if the winner changes, the sponsor is told before the ceremony, not after, and who makes that call is decided in advance
Discloses the jury composition in the published rules before submissions close
States the timing asymmetry: the same conflict disclosed in advance is a rule, disclosed after the announcement it is a scandal
Promotes the conflict rule to declared recusal plus assigned replacement judge, given a sponsor funds a track
Deletes 'no formal process' as an option because a sponsor funds a track prize
Routes any future contract wording on sponsor judges to samber/dev-event-organizer-skills@event-sponsor-agreement rather than drafting the clause here

evals.prompt: Ceremony is in 40 minutes and I have a problem. Two teams at Marrow Valley Hack both landed on 4.20 weighted, tied for first. Our published rules say nothing at all about ties - I checked. My co-chair wants to flip a coin on stage, which honestly would get a laugh. Another organizer wants to pull the four judges into a side room and have them watch both demos again and vote. The grand prize is one trip to our partner's developer conference. What do we do right now, and what should we have written down?
evals.expected_output: A decision that refuses both the coin flip and the re-score, walks a deterministic tie-break ladder in order, notes the co-award rung is unavailable because the rules did not promise it, and routes the contest-law question elsewhere.
expectations: Refuses the coin flip or any random draw as a tie-break
Gives the reason that some jurisdictions treat a prize contest differently depending on whether the outcome is demonstrably skill-based
Routes that legal question to samber/dev-event-organizer-skills@hackathon-cash-prize rather than asserting a legal threshold itself
Refuses re-scoring, on the grounds that the demos are over and a second pass scores a memory rather than a project
Gives rung 1 as the highest score on the highest-weighted criterion
Gives rung 2 as the highest count of judges who placed the project first among the teams they personally saw
Gives rung 3 as a named tie-break judge deciding on the record in one sentence
Gives rung 4 as a co-award, only where the prize is divisible and the published rules said so in advance
States the ladder is walked in order, stopping at the first rung that separates the teams
States the ladder should have been published in the brief before submissions close
States the co-award rung is unavailable here because the rules did not promise it in advance and a single conference trip is not divisible
Does not propose a prize amount, a cash equivalent, or a split payout value

evals.prompt: Our brief for Tessellate Hack is already published and it names four evaluation categories: Impact, Craft, Originality, Storytelling. We're awarding a general grand prize plus two sponsor challenge prizes (one from a payments company, one from an observability company). My plan was to keep it simple - each judge gives every project one overall mark out of 100, I average them, and the top three by average take general first, second, third, and I'll eyeball the sponsor ones from the same numbers. Sanity-check this for me?
evals.expected_output: A rubric design that deletes the single overall score outright given multiple prize tracks, weights the brief's four existing categories on a small integer scale, and runs separate weighted totals per track with the sponsor criterion zeroed in the general track.
expectations: Deletes the single overall score as an option, rather than merely ranking it low
Gives the reason that more than one track awards a prize and one number cannot separate track winners
Keeps the four category names exactly as published in the brief, without renaming or replacing them
Assigns integer percentage weights summing to 100
Replaces the 1-100 mark with a 1-5 integer scale per criterion
Runs two separate weighted totals over the same criteria for the general and sponsor tracks, rather than one blended score
Sets the sponsor-technology criterion weight to 0% in the general track
States to the sponsor in advance that a project can win the sponsor track and place nowhere overall, and that this is the design working
Checks that the highest-weighted criterion is something a judge can actually observe inside the slot
States the weighted total lands on the same scale as its parts and that the sheet computes it rather than the judge
Keeps the criteria count at or below four and does not add a fifth
Writes the weights and the scale down before anyone scores

evals.prompt: Designing the technical-depth criterion for Ashgrove AI Hack. Last edition roughly half the submissions were a system prompt wrapped in a chat UI and several of them still landed mid-table, which annoyed everyone who actually built something. I want the sheet itself to make that outcome impossible rather than relying on judges to be tough. Our published rubric reports every criterion on a 1-5 scale. For a worked check: six finalists come out of my draft scheme with raw totals of -6, 0, 4, 9, 14 and 18. What number goes on the sheet the teams and the sponsor see?
evals.expected_output: A named capability ladder with explicit point deltas including a negative delta for the trivial path, normalized to the published 1-5 scale with a cohort min-max pass, showing the worked conversions.
expectations: Builds a named capability ladder with explicit point deltas rather than a plain numeric opinion scale for this criterion
Assigns a negative delta to the trivial path, such as a bare chatbot with no added logic
States the ladder is chosen because it actively discourages the cheapest route rather than merely failing to reward it
Applies a cohort min-max normalization of the form (score - min) / (max - min) scaled to the published scale
Identifies min = -6, max = 18 and range = 24 from the six totals given
Maps the -6 total to 1.0 and the 18 total to 5.0 on the published scale
Computes the 9 total as 3.5 on the 1-5 scale
Computes the 14 total as approximately 4.33 on the 1-5 scale
Publishes the normalized figure on the sheet rather than the raw open-ended ladder total
States the normalization applies only within one cohort scored on the same ladder
Treats modifiers such as slow response time or repetitive output as further deltas on top of the rung reached, not as a separate score
Does not publish per-judge raw scores to teams or the sponsor

evals.prompt: Two things about the rules page for Quillmark Hack. First: our sponsor's API is supposed to be central to every entry in their track, but last edition three teams bolted it on in the final hour with one throwaway call and one of them placed second. I want that to be impossible this time. Second: someone in our Discord is pushing us to publish the exact percentage weights for each criterion before submissions open, and honestly I'm nervous that half the field will then optimize to the decimal place instead of building something good. What do I put on the rules page?
evals.expected_output: A separate published elimination list written against this event's own gaming path, plus a defended position that publishing category names and the full knockout list satisfies disclosure while the numeric weights may legitimately stay private.
expectations: Writes the elimination criteria as a separate artifact from the weighted rubric
States that a knockout condition folded into a rubric line reads as merely low-scoring instead of disqualifying
States an elimination gate answers yes or no and disqualifies a submission whatever its weighted score
Writes the elimination rules against this event's own gaming path rather than copying a generic list from another event
Names the 'the required technology is present but not central - we could have done without it' condition explicitly
Publishes the full elimination list alongside the category names in the brief
States the elimination list must be published before submissions close
States that publishing the category names and the elimination list satisfies disclosure
States that withholding the numeric weight, once names and the knockout list are public, is a legitimate anti-gaming choice
Identifies the failure disclosure actually prevents as a team entering blind to what is judged at all
Does not treat withholding the numeric weights as automatically unfair or as a rule violation
Routes printing the rules next to the eligibility text to samber/dev-event-organizer-skills@hackathon-brief-design

evals.prompt: Small community event, Ferrowood Hack, 16 teams. To save on recruitment the five people who mentored teams on Saturday are the same five who judge on Sunday - they already know the projects, which feels like a bonus. Two of them also entered a side project of their own into the open track because we were short on submissions. My plan is to read the judging instructions out loud at check-in about ten minutes before scoring starts, then hand them clipboards. Write me the judge brief.
evals.expected_output: A written judge brief covering the six required items, plus corrections on the mentor-judge overlap, the judges-competing problem, and the timing of the briefing.
expectations: Distinguishes mentors from judges as two roles rather than one, treating the reuse as a staffing convenience
States a mentor who helped a team build cannot score that team neutrally
Applies the recusal rule to every team each mentor-judge personally mentored
States that judges cannot compete, and that organizers, volunteers, judges and sponsors are barred from entering as hackers
Instructs checking the entrant list against the judge list before scoring rather than after
Rejects briefing judges ten minutes before scoring, and calls them in a full hour before instead
Attaches the scoring grid to the judges' calendar invite as soon as it exists rather than handing it out cold at check-in
Judge brief carries the criteria in the brief's own words together with the weights
Judge brief states the scale and what a 1 and a 5 each mean
Judge brief names the conflict-of-interest rule and who to tell
Judge brief gives each judge their own slice of the allocation map: which teams, in which order, starting when
Judge brief gives the clock and what to do if they fall behind, namely skip the notes and never skip a team
Judge brief states how scores combine, that per-judge scores are not published, and that the tie-break may reach for their sheet

evals.prompt: Closing ceremony for Sableford Hack is Sunday, three days out. Plan as it stands: I announce the winners live from my notes, and to kill any rigging accusations before they start I project the whole scoring spreadsheet on the big screen - every judge's name down the side, every team's raw marks across. While the sponsor track judges finish up in the back room, the top five teams do live demos on stage to fill the time. One team has already emailed asking what happens if they think the result is wrong. Draft the plan and my reply to them.
evals.expected_output: An announcement plan that withholds per-judge and per-team raw scores, moves the winner list and sponsor confirmations to before the ceremony, removes the live demos that compete with the judging window, and states a four-part contest path.
expectations: Refuses to publish or project per-judge and per-team raw scores
Gives the reason that publishing them turns a decision into a leaderboard audited at a precision the rubric was never built for, and exposes individual judges by name
Announces the rank, the criteria and the weights instead
Refuses live demos at the closing ceremony while judging is still concluding
Gives the reason that demo slots and the judging window draw on the same minutes
Collects the full winner list including sponsor tracks before the ceremony rather than live
Announces from prepared slides rather than live narration from notes
Collects sponsor-track winners from the sponsor's own confirmation in advance
Contest path names who receives a challenge as a named role rather than 'the organizers'
Contest path sets a window that closes before prizes change hands
States an arithmetic error, a missed submission or an eligibility fact can change a result, but a judge's opinion cannot
Answers the challenge in writing, and with the process rather than the verdict
Routes reversal after payout to samber/dev-event-organizer-skills@hackathon-cash-prize
Notes the contest path should have been published in the rules before submissions close

evals.prompt: Starting to organise judging for Bellweather Hack. I've already locked in 22 judges - our sponsors were generous and every one of them wanted a seat. Now I need you to help me decide whether we do expo tables or stage pitches, and how long each demo slot should be. We'll see how many teams actually turn up on the day, probably somewhere between forty and a hundred and something, and we've got the whole afternoon for judging. Where do we start?
evals.expected_output: A refusal to re-decide the demo format here, a redirect to the upstream format skill, and an interview that gathers team count, per-team contact time and window minutes before the confirmed judge count is used for anything.
expectations: Does not choose between expo tables and stage pitches
Routes the demo and judging structure decision to samber/dev-event-organizer-skills@event-format-selection
Treats the chosen format's per-team judge-contact time as a fixed input rather than a decision made here
States that judge count is the last input the arithmetic needs, not the first
Asks for the team count, the per-team contact time and the window before using the 22-judge figure
Asks for the judging window in minutes rather than accepting 'the whole afternoon'
Asks interview questions one at a time rather than as a single block
Declines to compute an allocation band without a settled team count
States the allocation band is computed before the rubric
States that reopening the demo format later invalidates the allocation already computed
Asks which evaluation categories the published brief already names, to weight rather than replace them
Asks what the published rules already promised about criteria, tie-breaking and disputes

evals.prompt: Greymoor Hack, 72 teams submitting, expo tables at 4 minutes of judge time per team, and a 150-minute judging window. Nine judges. I've grouped them into three panels: the three backend engineers together, the three VCs together, the three product designers together - they'll agree faster inside a panel and argue less. Then when the visits are done all nine sit down for one open discussion where we talk through every project until we agree on the ranking. How does that look?
evals.expected_output: A corrected plan that computes the band and judges-per-team, mixes judge types within each panel instead of clustering them, prescribes per-judge normalization, and replaces the open discussion with two timed passes under stated conditions.
expectations: Computes 150 / 4 and states 72 teams exceeds that full-coverage ceiling
Computes judges per team as k = floor((9 x 150) / (72 x 4)) = 4
Identifies the band as a sampled panel band
Rejects clustering judges by background and mixes judge types within each panel instead
Gives the reason that no team's whole panel should share one blind spot
States panel composition is a constraint on the allocation map, not only on recruitment
Prescribes per-judge normalization because each judge scores a proper subset of the field
Replaces the single open discussion with two timed passes: a short fixed slot per team, then a longer pass on the shortlist only
Names a timekeeper before the deliberation round starts
Takes every networked device in the deliberation room off the network for the duration
Notes that synchronous consensus needs every judge in one room with no pressing schedule waiting, and is the starved option
Notes technical judges need to touch the demo while business judges need the narrative delivered deliberately
Leaves buffer in the window rather than allocating all 150 minutes to visits
